summary:
Haiti does not criminalise same-sex conduct; the prohibition has been off the books since 1791. The legal framework provides no recognition of gender identity, no statutory anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity or sexual orientation, and no hate-crime enhancement. The judiciary does not function as a protection avenue in practice.

The legislature has twice moved to tighten the regime. In August 2017 the Haitian Senate passed a bill banning same-sex marriage and public LGBT advocacy, carrying up to three years' imprisonment and a fine of about US$8,000 for the parties. A June 2017 Senate bill would allow denial of the Certificat de Bonne Vie et Moeurs, the good-conduct certificate that employers and universities require, on grounds of homosexuality. Both measures awaited a vote in the Chamber of Deputies as of November 2017.

The certificate itself already operates against LGBT people: it lists homosexuality as a crime that can justify refusal, which directly affects students and job seekers, and the June 2017 bill was drafted to regulate who receives it. No procedure for legal gender recognition exists, so a visitor's documents will carry the sex marker assigned at issuance.

Visible trans and gender-nonconforming people face a documented hostile climate. The US State Department's 2018 report recorded that attitudes in Haiti "remained hostile toward LGBTI individuals who were public and visible about their sexual orientation or gender identity and expression, particularly in Port-au-Prince." Charlot Jeudy, president of Kouraj, the national LGBTQ advocacy organisation, was found dead at his home in Port-au-Prince on 25 November 2019; press reports cited unconfirmed poisoning, and ILGALAC issued a mourning statement. Transgender people have faced documented harassment in the post-earthquake displacement camps.

No prison-placement practice is documented for trans detainees: there is no known rule assigning housing by birth sex versus identity, no separate units, and no recorded solitary or segregation practice. That absence reflects a lack of documentation rather than a guaranteed placement outcome.

Constitutional guarantees of health care, housing, education, food and social security apply to all citizens, but LGBTQ people routinely conceal their orientation or gender identity for fear of discrimination, which impedes access. After the 2010 earthquake, gay and bisexual men reported adopting a more masculine demeanor to avoid harassment and to reduce the chances of being denied emergency housing, health care and food-for-work programs.
